After the mistrial, while prosecutors talked about continuing the case, someone shouted, "You only cared when the kids were dead. Why didn't you care about the mother?"
I read that sentence over and over.
Because the kids were dead.
Of course we should care about a mother in psychiatric crisis. We should care long before she reaches the point of hurting herself or her children. We should care enough to catch the warning signs, take families seriously and get treatment in place while it can still save lives.
But once three children have been killed, I refuse to accept that putting those children at the center somehow means we lack compassion for women.
Something is badly wrong when that even has to be said.
And this isn't happening in isolation.
In just the last several months, there have been case after case involving children killed by their mothers or in alleged murder-suicides involving their mothers. In Massachusetts, two children were found dead and their mother was charged with their murders. In Arizona, police say a mother shot and killed her 10-year-old son and 18-month-old daughter before killing herself. In Texas, police say a mother shot her two young children and then herself.
Then there is New York. Four siblings, ages 13, 11 and 10-year-old twins, were found dead in June in what police described as a planned murder-suicide involving their mother and grandmother.
Four children in one family.
And now there is a two-year-old little boy named Barrett in Illinois.
Barrett's case should make all of us uneasy.
Prosecutors say his mother, Corie Walsh, had gotten deeply invested in the Clancy trial. They say she was texting friends about it just hours before Barrett was found hanging in the basement. She has been charged with first-degree murder. Those allegations have not been proven in court.
I'm not saying Lindsay Clancy caused Barrett Walsh's death. There's no evidence of that, and it would be wrong to claim it.
But I am asking if anyone is willing to look at the culture we're building around these cases.
PolitiBrawl is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, please consider becoming a paid subscriber.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..v6hZFP83q1HsJZpjCNG-9H8kq_rR2YcJ3NvNCU4Kq8Q?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=214571286)
We know how people work. Notoriety matters. Social media amplifies things. Strangers form communities around people they've never met. Defendants turn into celebrities. Trials turn into entertainment. Algorithms take the darkest things that happen and turn them into movements.
So what happens when a woman who killed her three children stops being just a defendant whose mental state needs careful attention and becomes a symbol instead?
What happens when people show up in matching colors for her? When thousands of strangers start identifying with her? When the entire story becomes Lindsay's pain, her illness, her treatment, her defense, her supporters, her future?
Where are Cora, Dawson and Callan?
There's another question almost no one wants to touch.
What if Lindsay Clancy had been a man?
Picture a father who strangled his five-year-old daughter, his three-year-old son and his eight-month-old baby.
Now picture hundreds of men outside the courthouse in matching shirts standing with him. Heart signs. Applause for his lawyer. Posts everywhere about how other fathers deeply relate to him. People raising money and organizing around his cause.
Would we call that compassion?
Or would it sicken us?
We already know the answer.
Women deserve compassion. Mothers deserve compassion. Women in the grip of postpartum psychiatric illness need compassion and real treatment.
But compassion does not mean we go blind.
My Christian faith keeps telling me something this culture seems less and less able to hold. Mercy and truth are not opposites. You can have deep compassion for a broken person and still refuse to pretend that what happened was anything less than evil and horrific.
Jesus never taught us to get to mercy by throwing out the truth.
There's a truth here that should sit above politics, ideology, gender and every debate about mental health.
Children are precious.
They are defenseless.
They are supposed to be safe with us.
A five-year-old can't speak for herself. A three-year-old can't organize a rally. An eight-month-old can't tell us what happened. A two-year-old can't describe his fear.
They can't post on TikTok. They can't do interviews. They can't talk about their trauma or build a following or give their side of the story.
They're dead.
We're the only voices they have left.
That's why I will not take part in any conversation that turns murdered children into background characters in the story of the adult who killed them.
Talk about postpartum psychosis. We should.
Push for better treatment. Yes.
Ask the hard questions about criminal responsibility. That's what courts are for.
Have compassion for Lindsay Clancy. My faith requires it even when it's hard.
But do not turn her into a hero.
Do not build a movement around the person who murdered the children.
And stop asking why some of us keep talking about the kids.
Cora.
Dawson.
Callan.
Barrett.
And all the others whose names most people will never hear.
Their mothers have plenty of advocates.
**The children need witnesses.**
**I will stand with the children.**

But I cannot watch what is happening around the Lindsay Clancy case and stay silent. Cora was five. Dawson was three. Callan was eight months old. Their mother killed them. Those are the facts that should stop us cold. Instead, I've watched hundreds of people gather outside a courthouse dressed in pink to support Lindsay Clancy. I've watched them make hearts with their hands. I've watched her attorney get applauded. I've read post after post full of sympathy and identification that centers almost completely on her suffering while three small children are already dead. And I keep asking the same question. Where are the children? I understand compassion. I understand mental illness. I understand that postpartum psychosis is real and can destroy a person. I understand that criminal responsibility and moral horror aren't always the same legal question. I'm an attorney. I don't need anyone explaining the insanity defense to me. I'm also a mother. And three children are dead. There comes a point where compassion gets so twisted that we lose the innocent. I think we've hit it. We should care long before she reaches the point of hurting herself or her children. We should care enough to catch the warning signs, take families seriously and get treatment in place while it can still save lives. But once three children have been killed, I refuse to accept that putting those children at the center somehow means we lack compassion for women. Something is badly wrong when that even has to be said. And this isn't happening in isolation. In just the last several months, there have been case after case involving children killed by their mothers or in alleged murder-suicides involving their mothers. In Massachusetts, two children were found dead and their mother was charged with their murders. In Arizona, police say a mother shot and killed her 10-year-old son and 18-month-old daughter before killing herself. In Texas, police say a mother shot her two young children and then herself. Then there is New York. Four siblings, ages 13, 11 and 10-year-old twins, were found dead in June in what police described as a planned murder-suicide involving their mother and grandmother. Four children in one family. And now there is a two-year-old little boy named Barrett in Illinois. Barrett's case should make all of us uneasy. Prosecutors say his mother, Corie Walsh, had gotten deeply invested in the Clancy trial. They say she was texting friends about it just hours before Barrett was found hanging in the basement. She has been charged with first-degree murder. Those allegations have not been proven in court. I'm not saying Lindsay Clancy caused Barrett Walsh's death. | Patriot, Last October, my phone buzzed with a text I almost ignored. I saw the area code and thought it was a spam call from Beijing. I wasn't about to answer that. The next day, I found out it was real. President Trump wanted to meet with me at the White House. I figured it might be something military-related, so I flew up for a sit-down with the Commander-in-Chief. I walked into the Oval Office and shook his hand. **He's known for that handshake of his.** _I gave him the farm boy handshake from Kentucky,_ and he gave me the New York construction site handshake right back, right there over the Resolute Desk. | [ ](http://links.justandfreegop.com/u/click?_t=8ca5ef3d31cc43bcb1fbe6968d953911&_m=a028f3bdde1448819963a14085d7d659&_e=S19RAgcU4Z4tw0JJJOq8zGtuRI9DnEF_Ni-Rt4Xxic7vxlay5BxN0dI3tWmnqAnZmJMHQx7g8HTGfBCc0i3H_CUM-42Zfk_R1_jg_qHlczQKulueHE9ukav3i9HM_qY3yYlACxryoL1TN1r1f-kfV6ogQrNmO9oGcUzWO3cHwmjbJs8Zh0E3thyC2BU2LSe3j14wd65nRyrF5Ec2YpLVZ5HWc7v1QXaXTSBmWa4j-2ctOmtdvw1X-1QcHE0QehI1aHACaj_ox8sOLTUz48lkbT3I9HR2PP3C5LT3o0dLdJiK2PZ0nGbqqc1qDSJz_s_o-h5MmVU9fWS8dxUihnK-BtPSkop4O-vhB007oqRSkTBW9TXOYFx3N8vZMNfOgW2u7ata1CJ0i3A0uCzjjt1j6jJmKKnCTcEgIrGYHUjEF5TJGvicEpOpuVLX1XB9poVny3st7a7LPIJ6-F72h8xy9yHkZ6h0PzadfLBE0yZyDLTkbwof03R0ThK6WH0nvtt-wbOgCU_qaLBvjhSvm06mjwEcpaQprJstAn5sJHFM34Haza2Y6ef4Tz3fMeMuHBdusSx8W2-qhHXT8YpRqDH0Zz_dB8vxju-FhRuHgxYykPRl--uem9f3eEc9TAC82Mgc-hlkuFOSSRkeRlRkOd4kSiAa0Iu_K5GQFk3_4R77HfM2gA83wBoZ-dknxq9rNMg2LJ2QJCDFD9inyXMmO7b-HUqabRG_XFUHLdMttup_gS23m8-w3_MCZ9yGdPTuyGIglDTTn5_62w3-y2rqqFW3oYt9BNbu20NDHfxBb129fvR7JD9qDxhiVnqo0uEDVBnvGL1F41koCckeEYG1G1nDlNFlWm3-TlFyd-oSmXMWdtgKleOdR1uXBWNqWr-W1ZyN4G0-wt2H1hRlUQPeT6jOkGbm7FzqbJH-jcFWL1LCpAjbxR8z03hamB8akO8-fW7r)

He had a classified briefing book on the desk with my life and military record in it. He opened it up and said, _“Ed, you've got a lot of college.”_
**I told him I never liked college much. I'm more of a doer.**
We talked for about 35 minutes. The whole time, Zelensky was sitting and waiting in his motorcade while the next room was filled with every cabinet official the President had... waiting while we talked – but it was important; it was about the future of our Nation.
By the end of it, he told me to go home, talk to my family, pray, and consider serving my Nation again by running for Congress.
I went home. I thought about it; I talked with Family – and I prayed hard.
**[This summer, I beat a seven-term incumbent by ten points in the most expensive primary in House history.](http://links.justandfreegop.com/u/click?_t=8ca5ef3d31cc43bcb1fbe6968d953911&_m=a028f3bdde1448819963a14085d7d659&_e=S19RAgcU4Z4tw0JJJOq8zGtuRI9DnEF_Ni-Rt4Xxic7vxlay5BxN0dI3tWmnqAnZmJMHQx7g8HTGfBCc0i3H_CUM-42Zfk_R1_jg_qHlczQKulueHE9ukav3i9HM_qY3yYlACxryoL1TN1r1f-kfV6ogQrNmO9oGcUzWO3cHwmjbJs8Zh0E3thyC2BU2LSe3j14wd65nRyrF5Ec2YpLVZ5HWc7v1QXaXTSBmWa4j-2ctOmtdvw1X-1QcHE0QehI1aHACaj_ox8sOLTUz48lkbT3I9HR2PP3C5LT3o0dLdJiK2PZ0nGbqqc1qDSJz_s_o-h5MmVU9fWS8dxUihnK-BtPSkop4O-vhB007oqRSkTBFZ_B4qkkxuW05FRpqyReU6Sy3tcYM3BonFiXxvmvJFDEQY5YokWDghkqosgd2YGP0gtyyFG1anT1zxsHyvxNgdYEdhVPIEoqA6cALR-5c6PFUQy2GLG7q1Z37GTXHlMKR1FnyY8BxIC9hmXFbwk-ma6-lKARNcguTomY5YnStlg-ebRg6sL83tsw56iivVg7O-1qOPEx_MrcrEqyG6abCt1vNkysrkqz9o7SrmWvuTrLefPyffpEdeTHz2uE2r5s5FvHWh1rcVnV-WRhmy2A8H_GzkkYBWFFY-dlIZ2j5vnnbvVNfHM7An7tNuXQV4qhybWpK1RidqzD7SPEH2RE_HEMDEYC8AVhpNDnw7pZdJmnSJR960zZUsVwqZMDk_ofmfOgEBuJhdelJ7jdfyrfyvbjC3Xzl35QhUHQnBKUM_D6pMMklgYjNuyfEwAsO1NwfgdWEQXkZ1lCM1pUhww_bxYlYCZlBKkMixYtK8mpK2lkBvWcPE2y-ZyBy2vLzii3q_7bWOe-VTzrnXexrkwE9-_kSanDMWnZqBB087_j5coD5wSLfHo9v4Y_LITfYuQhwfnmimK4Ltsh6WLuducUn)**

Here's what that Oval Office meeting meant to me... and why it matters to you.
**President Trump isn't just trying to win elections. He's trying to finish the job – for us.**
_Secure the border. Rebuild the economy. Restore American strength. And he cannot do any of it without a House that's got his back and ours on every single vote._
**That's why he came looking for fighters, not politicians.**
Every seat matters. Lose enough of them and the agenda stalls. The spending continues. The border opens back up. Radical Democrats dismantle our Nation before our very eyes. _Everything we've fought for goes into reverse._
Kentucky's 4th is one of those seats, and Democrats know it.
The moment we secured the Republican nomination, the other side started making calls. They know we came out of a brutal, expensive primary with our account nearly wiped out. _They are going to pour outside money into this district to flip it, slow Trump down, and send a message that his movement for us is losing steam._
We have a narrow window right now, before their money arrives and their ads go up in the final weeks, **[to build the grassroots foundation this campaign needs to keep fighting and WIN in November.](http://links.justandfreegop.com/u/click?_t=8ca5ef3d31cc43bcb1fbe6968d953911&_m=a028f3bdde1448819963a14085d7d659&_e=S19RAgcU4Z4tw0JJJOq8zGtuRI9DnEF_Ni-Rt4Xxic7vxlay5BxN0dI3tWmnqAnZmJMHQx7g8HTGfBCc0i3H_CUM-42Zfk_R1_jg_qHlczQKulueHE9ukav3i9HM_qY3yYlACxryoL1TN1r1f-kfV6ogQrNmO9oGcUzWO3cHwmjbJs8Zh0E3thyC2BU2LSe3j14wd65nRyrF5Ec2YpLVZ5HWc7v1QXaXTSBmWa4j-2ctOmtdvw1X-1QcHE0QehI1aHACaj_ox8sOLTUz48lkbT3I9HR2PP3C5LT3o0dLdJiK2PZ0nGbqqc1qDSJz_s_o-h5MmVU9fWS8dxUihnK-BtPSkop4O-vhB007oqRSkTBzL-SB2pwwjJ9KwS2mDD7a6ayHnWcp1qSj93gA1_-_K5if3uSEVpWF7TnpVy5Vc8jedxnxMYFS5gSNWW2N75wFinBKVFEIbH_-Ln5hcwlwonYH_AUDmfIW9wyyV47IPJ8WaL6CNcsPxMvzuOH-s5VRUbOqkfsPKZbJi4KTNhahlDFnBp091WXyJpJL2boozHXLDbWAVydfhNC2zadtdx1riLfyj6jhuW0HeHxcnzVwh5aAfda0I5rcVin0UyFvtvdwtETbKLmusaAwg650DFNrZOjlfAZZmK-x_eok8ERQkXI6tArGIy3jQebEkWwCcO85QicAqyWAr3of8rnMiBtoDH7u_qDIgNhGOPqHAm1v3YLP-4QYcCELwjO4nzQftdqzL3vtqH9i4yti6gjj7gtUhQDQ7Rdj48GC09tQ-uu_ATtk2Ho8BjBVXqOKLckfmXTu6zZEt7lmJUfrQdPrS-yHe2RsEdJ1MB_vHVR7MODHt_PHhpGr1gqqBLG7kZziBILswUQDHldEj0OoBY4ateqzXxfP61CXvJp6X0TF65VbApMHpkTN9_AKyXuUkSy64PYox7J7v2aBCNxp_bFNSkXl)**
**If we don't close that gap fast, we hand them exactly the opening they're looking for.**
_President Trump picked this District. He picked this fight. And he picked a fifth-generation Kentucky farmer and career active-duty Navy SEAL Officer and Army Ranger-qualified patriot to face the radical Democrats._

clean_body: | Patriot, Last October, my phone buzzed with a text I almost ignored. I saw the area code and thought it was a spam call from Beijing. I wasn't about to answer that. The next day, I found out it was real. President Trump wanted to meet with me at the White House. I figured it might be something military-related, so I flew up for a sit-down with the Commander-in-Chief. I walked into the Oval Office and shook his hand. He's known for that handshake of his. I gave him the farm boy handshake from Kentucky, and he gave me the New York construction site handshake right back, right there over the Resolute Desk. | He had a classified briefing book on the desk with my life and military record in it. He opened it up and said, “Ed, you've got a lot of college.” I told him I never liked college much. I'm more of a doer. We talked for about 35 minutes. The whole time, Zelensky was sitting and waiting in his motorcade while the next room was filled with every cabinet official the President had... waiting while we talked – but it was important; it was about the future of our Nation. By the end of it, he told me to go home, talk to my family, pray, and consider serving my Nation again by running for Congress. I went home. I thought about it; I talked with Family – and I prayed hard. Here's what that Oval Office meeting meant to me... and why it matters to you. President Trump isn't just trying to win elections. He's trying to finish the job – for us. Secure the border. Rebuild the economy. Restore American strength. And he cannot do any of it without a House that's got his back and ours on every single vote. That's why he came looking for fighters, not politicians. Every seat matters. Lose enough of them and the agenda stalls. The spending continues. The border opens back up. Radical Democrats dismantle our Nation before our very eyes. Everything we've fought for goes into reverse. Kentucky's 4th is one of those seats, and Democrats know it. The moment we secured the Republican nomination, the other side started making calls. They know we came out of a brutal, expensive primary with our account nearly wiped out. They are going to pour outside money into this district to flip it, slow Trump down, and send a message that his movement for us is losing steam. We have a narrow window right now, before their money arrives and their ads go up in the final weeks, If we don't close that gap fast, we hand them exactly the opening they're looking for. President Trump picked this District. He picked this fight. And he picked a fifth-generation Kentucky farmer and career active-duty Navy SEAL Officer and Army Ranger-qualified patriot to face the radical Democrats. I'm not going to let him down. But I need you in this fight with me right now - we are on a no-fail mission together. Farm Strong. SEAL Tough. America First. Kentucky Always! Ed Gallrein Republican Nominee | Kentucky's 4th Congressional District | Paid for by Gallrein for Congress PO Box 1059, Shelbyville, KY 40066 |

There is an interesting moment happening in American health.

For most of my thirty years coaching people, weight loss has been sold through some variation of the same promise: eat this instead of that, count these calories, eliminate this food group, buy this supplement, follow this program. The details changed, the villains changed, and every few years the cover of the diet book changed, but the basic proposition remained remarkably consistent.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/cd843387-0006-4f68-a204-438e513a3473?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Then came the injection.

Suddenly, millions of people discovered they could dramatically reduce their appetite without having to negotiate with it. Food became less interesting. Portions became smaller. The incessant chatter some people describe as "food noise" quieted. Weight began disappearing, sometimes at a rate people had never been able to achieve through dieting.

After decades of working with people who have struggled with obesity, I understand the appeal. I have spent my professional life sitting across from real human beings, not metabolic equations. I know what it looks like when someone fights the same twenty, fifty, or one hundred pounds for years. I know the embarrassment hidden behind a joke before stepping on a scale and the quiet shame that sometimes keeps someone away from a swimming pool, family photograph, or doctor's appointment.

So my objection to the GLP-1 revolution does not come from a lack of empathy.

It comes from thirty years of it.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/cca97de2-d13c-45d6-b2a6-61a1ce13ea36?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
I am fascinated by physiology, but I am equally fascinated by human behavior. Eventually you discover that health does not happen in a laboratory. It happens on Monday morning when the alarm rings. It happens at the restaurant when everyone else orders dessert. It happens when you are tired, stressed, traveling, lonely, celebrating, grieving, bored, or standing in your kitchen at 9:30 at night.

Human beings do not merely have metabolisms. We have habits.

That is why I believe the most important question surrounding today's pharmaceutical weight-loss revolution is not whether these drugs can make people lighter.

They clearly can.

The more important question is: **What kind of health are we actually trying to build?**

**The Biology Was Already There**
There is an irony hiding in the name GLP-1.

Glucagon-like peptide-1 is not a pharmaceutical invention. It is part of normal human physiology.

Our intestinal system naturally releases GLP-1 in response to food. It participates in an intricate conversation among the gut, pancreas, brain, and other tissues, influencing insulin secretion, glucagon signaling, appetite, satiety, and food intake.

Modern GLP-1 medications work because scientists learned how to amplify or imitate biological signaling systems the human body already possesses.

That is remarkable pharmacology.

It should also produce a little humility.

The pharmaceutical industry did not invent satiety; it learned how to manipulate a system of satiety that was already there. And for all the complexity of receptors, hormones, and signaling pathways, much of the resulting weight loss ultimately comes down to something simple:

People eat less.

That is precisely where my concern begins.

Reducing appetite is not the same thing as teaching someone how to eat. Reducing energy intake is not the same thing as developing metabolic health, and losing weight is certainly not the same thing as building a strong human being.

I have never been interested in merely making people smaller.
**The Scale Tells an Incomplete Story**
The bathroom scale is one of the most persuasive liars in health and fitness.

Not because the number is false. The number is perfectly accurate.

The problem is everything it refuses to tell you.

A scale cannot distinguish a pound of fat from a pound of skeletal muscle. It cannot tell you whether your legs are stronger, whether you can get off the floor without using your hands, whether your balance is improving, whether you can carry your suitcase through an airport at seventy-five, or whether you are slowly becoming a lighter but more fragile version of yourself.

We have somehow reduced the extraordinarily complex concept of health to a single number produced by gravity.

That becomes especially important during rapid pharmaceutical weight loss.

Large trials of medications such as tirzepatide have shown tremendous reductions in body weight, much of it body fat. But meaningful losses of lean tissue occur as well. Lean mass is not synonymous with skeletal muscle, so we should not pretend every pound of lean mass measured by a scan is contractile muscle disappearing. But neither should we dismiss the issue.

Researchers and clinicians are increasingly emphasizing adequate protein intake and progressive resistance training during GLP-1-assisted weight loss precisely because muscle preservation matters.
And here is where physiology collides with human behavior.

Preserving muscle requires someone to consume enough high-quality protein despite a suppressed appetite, progressively load skeletal muscle, and train consistently enough to give the body a reason to preserve that tissue.

Could someone do all of this while taking a GLP-1 medication?

Of course.

But after three decades of coaching, I am interested in more than what is biologically possible.

I am interested in what human beings predictably do.

The person who has spent twenty years avoiding resistance training does not automatically become a disciplined strength trainee because a physician writes a prescription. The person who has never prioritized protein does not suddenly begin thinking about muscle protein synthesis because an injection made lunch less appealing.

A medication can alter a signal.

It cannot create a habit.
**Muscle Is Not Decoration**

I wish we would stop talking about muscle as though it were an accessory.

Muscle is usually discussed in the language of abs, arms, swimsuits, and vanity. Somewhere along the way, building muscle became associated with bodybuilders instead of human beings.

That is a profound misunderstanding of physiology.

Muscle allows us to produce force, absorb force, climb stairs, carry groceries, maintain balance, protect joints, regulate glucose more effectively, rise from a chair, play with grandchildren, and remain capable as we age.
Muscle is part of the architecture underneath longevity.

And muscle requires a reason to remain.

That reason is load.

I often tell my clients that the body is constantly listening.

Place bone under mechanical stress and it receives information. Challenge the cardiovascular system and it receives information. Expose muscle to meaningful resistance and it receives information.

The body adapts to the demands we repeatedly place upon it.

That is why resistance training occupies such an important role in the Fast.Eat.Live. philosophy. We are not simply trying to create an energy deficit. We want to preserve and build useful tissue.
We fast.

Then we return to nourishment.

We eat protein.

We train.

We recover.

The phases matter because the signals matter.

**The Other Fuel Tank**

There is another piece of physiology I believe our culture has almost completely forgotten.

Stored body fat is energy.

That sentence seems absurdly obvious, yet much of modern eating behavior suggests we no longer understand it.

A person can be carrying tens of thousands of calories of stored energy and still feel alarmed when breakfast is delayed by two hours.

We have normalized an eating environment our ancestors could scarcely have imagined: food available every waking hour, snacks carried everywhere, drive-through restaurants glowing at midnight, calorie-containing beverages between meals, office food, entertainment food, convenience food, and an entire economy designed to make stopping consumption surprisingly difficult.

Then we wonder why the body continues storing energy it is rarely given permission to retrieve.

Human metabolism was not built with one fuel source.

As fasting progresses, insulin falls, liver glycogen becomes less dominant, stored triglycerides are broken apart, fatty acids become available, and the liver begins converting increasing amounts of those fatty acids into ketone bodies.

The body changes fuel sources.

Researchers sometimes describe this as the metabolic switch.

Imagine owning a hybrid automobile with two energy systems and spending your entire life believing only one of them worked.

That is how many modern people live metabolically.

We have become extraordinarily practiced at consuming energy and surprisingly unfamiliar with accessing the energy already stored on our bodies.

Hunger arrives and immediately produces a behavioral response: _I need to eat._

But hunger is not always evidence of an energy emergency.

Sometimes it is simply a signal.

And one of the most empowering things a person can discover is that a signal does not have to become a command.

**What Fasting Teaches**
This is where fasting becomes more interesting to me than simple calorie reduction.
The person fasting still experiences hunger.

That matters.

The stomach growls. A familiar eating hour arrives. Someone walks into a restaurant. A coworker opens something that smells wonderful. The internal suggestion appears: _You could eat._

And the person practicing an intentional fast answers: _Yes, I could. But I have chosen not to yet._

There is tremendous psychological value in that exchange.

Not because hunger is virtuous and certainly not because misery earns metabolic points.

It matters because human beings become stronger when they discover that discomfort does not possess authority over them.

At first, many people treat hunger as though a fire alarm has gone off. Then they begin recognizing its rhythm. Hunger rises. Hunger falls. They drink some water. They take a walk. They return to work and discover they are still mentally capable, physically functional, and very much alive.

Something changes.

They no longer fear the sensation.

That is very different from pharmacologically reducing the sensation.

The distinction is subtle, but from the perspective of human behavior it is enormous.

Fasting gives someone an opportunity to experience appetite without automatically obeying it. It creates a small laboratory of self-regulation.

And that skill travels.

The person who discovers they can be hungry without becoming miserable may begin noticing the same pattern elsewhere. Fatigue does not always have to cancel a workout. Irritation does not have to spill onto the family. Wanting another drink does not require having one, and the urge to pick up a phone can be noticed without being obeyed.

The skill being practiced is larger than fasting:

Discomfort can be experienced without immediately reaching for relief.

This is not diet culture.

This is human formation.

**Fasting Is Not Starvation**

Enthusiasm, however, can become its own kind of stupidity.

If fasting is good, longer fasting must be better. If ketosis is interesting, more ketosis must be superior.

Human beings have a remarkable ability to take a useful principle and drive it into a ditch.

Fast.Eat.Live. was never built around starvation.

Any meaningful period of energy restriction requires us to think intelligently about muscle. Longer periods of fasting can increase protein breakdown and reduce lean tissue, which is one reason I believe fasting should exist inside a rhythm rather than becoming an endurance contest.

We fast, but then we deliberately return to nourishment. Protein matters when we eat. Resistance matters when we train. Sleep matters while the body repairs what training has asked it to build.

There is a time to withdraw food and allow stored energy to become useful. There is a time to provide amino acids, minerals, vitamins, fatty acids, and energy. There is a time to place tissue under load and ask it to adapt.

And there is a time to recover.
**You Cannot Inject Discipline**
One of the most revealing things about pharmaceutical weight loss is what happens when the medication is removed.

Follow-up studies of both semaglutide and tirzepatide have demonstrated substantial weight regain for many participants after treatment is stopped.

The conventional medical explanation is that obesity is a chronic disease and therefore chronic pharmaceutical treatment may be required.

I understand the logic.

But as a coach, I hear another question underneath it:

What did the person learn to do?

If the principal mechanism producing the outcome remains pharmacological appetite suppression, then removing the pharmacology predictably changes the environment that produced the outcome.

That does not mean someone using a GLP-1 medication is lazy, weak, or morally deficient. I reject that kind of thinking completely.

It means the mechanism matters.

I want to know what remains when the external intervention disappears.

Has the person learned how hunger actually behaves? Do they understand protein, strength training, sleep, stress, and satiety? Have they developed confidence in their ability to participate in their own health?

Those questions are difficult to capture on a pharmaceutical trial spreadsheet.

But they determine much of what happens during the next twenty years of someone's life.

Stewardship is inconvenient. Training requires time. Protein requires planning. Fasting occasionally requires sitting with hunger. Strength takes years.

Human beings have always been attracted to shortcuts, and modern commerce has become exceptionally skilled at selling them.

But some things cannot be outsourced.

You can outsource a training program.

You cannot outsource the repetitions.

And you can pharmacologically suppress appetite.

**You cannot inject discipline.**
**The Body Is Not Empty**
One of my favorite moments during a Fast.Eat.Live. fast occurs when someone tells me they are hungry.

I usually smile.

Not because I enjoy their discomfort.

Because I know what may happen next.

The sensation comes and goes. The body continues working. Energy remains available.

Eventually, they begin understanding the strange truth hiding in plain sight.

They are not empty.

They are carrying stored energy.

Their body has been saving it for precisely the circumstance they have intentionally created.

No breakfast arrived.

No lunch arrived.

The kitchen is temporarily closed.

So, the metabolic system begins opening another pantry.

Triglycerides stored inside adipose tissue are broken apart. Fatty acids become available. The liver begins producing more ketones. The person who thought they had "no energy because I haven't eaten" discovers that the human body has been carrying a reserve tank the entire time.

That discovery can change someone's relationship with hunger.

And perhaps what they recover is trust: trust in the adaptability of the body, in their ability to practice restraint, and in the knowledge that food will still be there--and may taste even better--when the fast ends.
**Stewardship and Transformation**
My Christian faith inevitably shapes the way I see all of this.

I do not believe the human body is an accident.

I studied kinesiology, exercise physiology, and biology before earning my degree in 1997, and I have spent the decades since coaching people and continuing to study nutrition, physiology, and human performance.

The longer I study the body, the less interested I become in reducing it to a machine.

Machines are crude compared with us.

The human body stores energy during abundance and retrieves it during absence. It remodels bone in response to stress. It builds muscle when repeatedly asked to produce force. It adapts to training, temperature, altitude, sleep, nutrition, stress, and recovery.

Adaptation is everywhere.

As a Christian, I see design in that adaptability.

Fasting appears throughout Scripture, although never as God's ancient weight-loss program. Its purpose was spiritual: repentance, prayer, preparation, grief, discernment, and the intentional quieting of one appetite to attend more closely to something greater.

Yet I find it fascinating that this ancient practice also exposes us to physiological states modern abundance has made increasingly rare.

Modern people can go decades without missing a meal.

Historically, that is unusual.

Perhaps the question is not why fasting feels strange today.

Perhaps the question is why uninterrupted eating feels normal.

I have no interest in romanticizing obesity or minimizing how difficult changing it can be.

I have coached people too long for that.

But empathy does not require lowering our expectations for human beings.

Sometimes love asks more of people because we believe there is more available to them.

I do not want to help someone become a smaller version of the same unhealthy person.

I want to help build someone stronger and more capable: a person who understands food and their own metabolism, protects muscle, values sleep and movement, can tolerate temporary discomfort, trains with confidence, and still knows how to gather around a table with gratitude and joy.

Health is not merely an outcome.

It is a practice.

As a Christian, I would call that stewardship.

As a coach, I would call it transformation.

And as a student of human physiology, I continue to be amazed by how often the path forward begins not by overpowering the body, but by finally learning how to work with it.

_**Before the shot, remember the fast.**_

What the GLP-1 Revolution Reveals About Appetite, Muscle, Metabolism, and the Biology We May Have Forgotten | | | Sep 7 | | | | | | | | | | | | There is an interesting moment happening in American health. For most of my thirty years coaching people, weight loss has been sold through some variation of the same promise: eat this instead of that, count these calories, eliminate this food group, buy this supplement, follow this program. The details changed, the villains changed, and every few years the cover of the diet book changed, but the basic proposition remained remarkably consistent. | | ---|---|--- Then came the injection. Suddenly, millions of people discovered they could dramatically reduce their appetite without having to negotiate with it. Food became less interesting. Portions became smaller. The incessant chatter some people describe as "food noise" quieted. Weight began disappearing, sometimes at a rate people had never been able to achieve through dieting. After decades of working with people who have struggled with obesity, I understand the appeal. I have spent my professional life sitting across from real human beings, not metabolic equations. I know what it looks like when someone fights the same twenty, fifty, or one hundred pounds for years. I know the embarrassment hidden behind a joke before stepping on a scale and the quiet shame that sometimes keeps someone away from a swimming pool, family photograph, or doctor's appointment. So my objection to the GLP-1 revolution does not come from a lack of empathy. It comes from thirty years of it. | | ---|---|--- I am fascinated by physiology, but I am equally fascinated by human behavior. Eventually you discover that health does not happen in a laboratory. It happens on Monday morning when the alarm rings. It happens at the restaurant when everyone else orders dessert. It happens when you are tired, stressed, traveling, lonely, celebrating, grieving, bored, or standing in your kitchen at 9:30 at night. Human beings do not merely have metabolisms. We have habits. That is why I believe the most important question surrounding today's pharmaceutical weight-loss revolution is not whether these drugs can make people lighter. They clearly can. The more important question is: What kind of health are we actually trying to build? The Biology Was Already There There is an irony hiding in the name GLP-1. Glucagon-like peptide-1 is not a pharmaceutical invention. It is part of normal human physiology. Our intestinal system naturally releases GLP-1 in response to food. It participates in an intricate conversation among the gut, pancreas, brain, and other tissues, influencing insulin secretion, glucagon signaling, appetite, satiety, and food intake. Modern GLP-1 medications work because scientists learned how to amplify or imitate biological signaling systems the human body already possesses. That is remarkable pharmacology. It should also produce a little humility. The pharmaceutical industry did not invent satiety; it learned how to manipulate a system of satiety that was already there. And for all the complexity of receptors, hormones, and signaling pathways, much of the resulting weight loss ultimately comes down to something simple: People eat less. That is precisely where my concern begins. Reducing appetite is not the same thing as teaching someone how to eat. Reducing energy intake is not the same thing as developing metabolic health, and losing weight is certainly not the same thing as building a strong human being. I have never been interested in merely making people smaller. The Scale Tells an Incomplete Story The bathroom scale is one of the most persuasive liars in health and fitness. Not because the number is false. The number is perfectly accurate. The problem is everything it refuses to tell you. A scale cannot distinguish a pound of fat from a pound of skeletal muscle. It cannot tell you whether your legs are stronger, whether you can get off the floor without using your hands, whether your balance is improving, whether you can carry your suitcase through an airport at seventy-five, or whether you are slowly becoming a lighter but more fragile version of yourself. We have somehow reduced the extraordinarily complex concept of health to a single number produced by gravity. That becomes especially important during rapid pharmaceutical weight loss. Large trials of medications such as tirzepatide have shown tremendous reductions in body weight, much of it body fat. But meaningful losses of lean tissue occur as well. Lean mass is not synonymous with skeletal muscle, so we should not pretend every pound of lean mass measured by a scan is contractile muscle disappearing. But neither should we dismiss the issue. Researchers and clinicians are increasingly emphasizing adequate protein intake and progressive resistance training during GLP-1-assisted weight loss precisely because muscle preservation matters. And here is where physiology collides with human behavior. Preserving muscle requires someone to consume enough high-quality protein despite a suppressed appetite, progressively load skeletal muscle, and train consistently enough to give the body a reason to preserve that tissue. Could someone do all of this while taking a GLP-1 medication? Of course. But after three decades of coaching, I am interested in more than what is biologically possible. I am interested in what human beings predictably do. The person who has spent twenty years avoiding resistance training does not automatically become a disciplined strength trainee because a physician writes a prescription. The person who has never prioritized protein does not suddenly begin thinking about muscle protein synthesis because an injection made lunch less appealing. A medication can alter a signal. It cannot create a habit. Muscle Is Not Decoration I wish we would stop talking about muscle as though it were an accessory. Muscle is usually discussed in the language of abs, arms, swimsuits, and vanity. Somewhere along the way, building muscle became associated with bodybuilders instead of human beings. That is a profound misunderstanding of physiology. Muscle allows us to produce force, absorb force, climb stairs, carry groceries, maintain balance, protect joints, regulate glucose more effectively, rise from a chair, play with grandchildren, and remain capable as we age. Muscle is part of the architecture underneath longevity. And muscle requires a reason to remain. That reason is load. I often tell my clients that the body is constantly listening. Place bone under mechanical stress and it receives information. Challenge the cardiovascular system and it receives information. Expose muscle to meaningful resistance and it receives information. The body adapts to the demands we repeatedly place upon it. That is why resistance training occupies such an important role in the Fast.Eat.Live. philosophy. We are not simply trying to create an energy deficit. We want to preserve and build useful tissue. We fast. Then we return to nourishment. We eat protein. We train. We recover. The phases matter because the signals matter. The Other Fuel Tank There is another piece of physiology I believe our culture has almost completely forgotten. Stored body fat is energy. That sentence seems absurdly obvious, yet much of modern eating behavior suggests we no longer understand it. A person can be carrying tens of thousands of calories of stored energy and still feel alarmed when breakfast is delayed by two hours. We have normalized an eating environment our ancestors could scarcely have imagined: food available every waking hour, snacks carried everywhere, drive-through restaurants glowing at midnight, calorie-containing beverages between meals, office food, entertainment food, convenience food, and an entire economy designed to make stopping consumption surprisingly difficult. Then we wonder why the body continues storing energy it is rarely given permission to retrieve. Human metabolism was not built with one fuel source. As fasting progresses, insulin falls, liver glycogen becomes less dominant, stored triglycerides are broken apart, fatty acids become available, and the liver begins converting increasing amounts of those fatty acids into ketone bodies. The body changes fuel sources. Researchers sometimes describe this as the metabolic switch. Imagine owning a hybrid automobile with two energy systems and spending your entire life believing only one of them worked. That is how many modern people live metabolically. We have become extraordinarily practiced at consuming energy and surprisingly unfamiliar with accessing the energy already stored on our bodies. Hunger arrives and immediately produces a behavioral response: I need to eat. But hunger is not always evidence of an energy emergency. Sometimes it is simply a signal. And one of the most empowering things a person can discover is that a signal does not have to become a command. What Fasting Teaches This is where fasting becomes more interesting to me than simple calorie reduction. The person fasting still experiences hunger. That matters. The stomach growls. A familiar eating hour arrives. Someone walks into a restaurant. A coworker opens something that smells wonderful. The internal suggestion appears: You could eat. And the person practicing an intentional fast answers: Yes, I could. But I have chosen not to yet. There is tremendous psychological value in that exchange. Not because hunger is virtuous and certainly not because misery earns metabolic points. It matters because human beings become stronger when they discover that discomfort does not possess authority over them. At first, many people treat hunger as though a fire alarm has gone off. Then they begin recognizing its rhythm. Hunger rises. Hunger falls. They drink some water. They take a walk. They return to work and discover they are still mentally capable, physically functional, and very much alive. Something changes. They no longer fear the sensation. That is very different from pharmacologically reducing the sensation. The distinction is subtle, but from the perspective of human behavior it is enormous. Fasting gives someone an opportunity to experience appetite without automatically obeying it. It creates a small laboratory of self-regulation. And that skill travels. The person who discovers they can be hungry without becoming miserable may begin noticing the same pattern elsewhere. Fatigue does not always have to cancel a workout. Irritation does not have to spill onto the family. Wanting another drink does not require having one, and the urge to pick up a phone can be noticed without being obeyed. The skill being practiced is larger than fasting: Discomfort can be experienced without immediately reaching for relief. This is not diet culture. This is human formation. Fasting Is Not Starvation Enthusiasm, however, can become its own kind of stupidity. If fasting is good, longer fasting must be better. If ketosis is interesting, more ketosis must be superior. Human beings have a remarkable ability to take a useful principle and drive it into a ditch. Fast.Eat.Live. was never built around starvation. Any meaningful period of energy restriction requires us to think intelligently about muscle. Longer periods of fasting can increase protein breakdown and reduce lean tissue, which is one reason I believe fasting should exist inside a rhythm rather than becoming an endurance contest. We fast, but then we deliberately return to nourishment. Protein matters when we eat. Resistance matters when we train. Sleep matters while the body repairs what training has asked it to build. There is a time to withdraw food and allow stored energy to become useful. There is a time to provide amino acids, minerals, vitamins, fatty acids, and energy. There is a time to place tissue under load and ask it to adapt. And there is a time to recover. You Cannot Inject Discipline One of the most revealing things about pharmaceutical weight loss is what happens when the medication is removed. Follow-up studies of both semaglutide and tirzepatide have demonstrated substantial weight regain for many participants after treatment is stopped. The conventional medical explanation is that obesity is a chronic disease and therefore chronic pharmaceutical treatment may be required. I understand the logic. But as a coach, I hear another question underneath it: What did the person learn to do? If the principal mechanism producing the outcome remains pharmacological appetite suppression, then removing the pharmacology predictably changes the environment that produced the outcome. That does not mean someone using a GLP-1 medication is lazy, weak, or morally deficient. I reject that kind of thinking completely. It means the mechanism matters. I want to know what remains when the external intervention disappears. Has the person learned how hunger actually behaves? Do they understand protein, strength training, sleep, stress, and satiety? Have they developed confidence in their ability to participate in their own health? Those questions are difficult to capture on a pharmaceutical trial spreadsheet. But they determine much of what happens during the next twenty years of someone's life. Stewardship is inconvenient. Training requires time. Protein requires planning. Fasting occasionally requires sitting with hunger. Strength takes years. Human beings have always been attracted to shortcuts, and modern commerce has become exceptionally skilled at selling them. But some things cannot be outsourced. You can outsource a training program. You cannot outsource the repetitions. And you can pharmacologically suppress appetite. You cannot inject discipline. The Body Is Not Empty One of my favorite moments during a Fast.Eat.Live. fast occurs when someone tells me they are hungry. I usually smile. Not because I enjoy their discomfort. Because I know what may happen next. The sensation comes and goes. The body continues working. Energy remains available. Eventually, they begin understanding the strange truth hiding in plain sight. They are not empty. They are carrying stored energy. Their body has been saving it for precisely the circumstance they have intentionally created. No breakfast arrived. No lunch arrived. The kitchen is temporarily closed. So, the metabolic system begins opening another pantry. Triglycerides stored inside adipose tissue are broken apart. Fatty acids become available. The liver begins producing more ketones. The person who thought they had "no energy because I haven't eaten" discovers that the human body has been carrying a reserve tank the entire time. That discovery can change someone's relationship with hunger. And perhaps what they recover is trust: trust in the adaptability of the body, in their ability to practice restraint, and in the knowledge that food will still be there--and may taste even better--when the fast ends. Stewardship and Transformation My Christian faith inevitably shapes the way I see all of this. I do not believe the human body is an accident. I studied kinesiology, exercise physiology, and biology before earning my degree in 1997, and I have spent the decades since coaching people and continuing to study nutrition, physiology, and human performance. The longer I study the body, the less interested I become in reducing it to a machine. Machines are crude compared with us. The human body stores energy during abundance and retrieves it during absence. It remodels bone in response to stress. It builds muscle when repeatedly asked to produce force. It adapts to training, temperature, altitude, sleep, nutrition, stress, and recovery. Adaptation is everywhere. As a Christian, I see design in that adaptability. Fasting appears throughout Scripture, although never as God's ancient weight-loss program. Its purpose was spiritual: repentance, prayer, preparation, grief, discernment, and the intentional quieting of one appetite to attend more closely to something greater. Yet I find it fascinating that this ancient practice also exposes us to physiological states modern abundance has made increasingly rare. Modern people can go decades without missing a meal. Historically, that is unusual. Perhaps the question is not why fasting feels strange today. Perhaps the question is why uninterrupted eating feels normal. I have no interest in romanticizing obesity or minimizing how difficult changing it can be. I have coached people too long for that. But empathy does not require lowering our expectations for human beings. Sometimes love asks more of people because we believe there is more available to them. I do not want to help someone become a smaller version of the same unhealthy person. I want to help build someone stronger and more capable: a person who understands food and their own metabolism, protects muscle, values sleep and movement, can tolerate temporary discomfort, trains with confidence, and still knows how to gather around a table with gratitude and joy. Health is not merely an outcome. It is a practice. As a Christian, I would call that stewardship. As a coach, I would call it transformation. And as a student of human physiology, I continue to be amazed by how often the path forward begins not by overpowering the body, but by finally learning how to work with it. Before the shot, remember the fast. | | ---|---|--- Editorial comments expressed in this column are the sole opinion of the writer. clean_body: I'm proud to stand with Darline Graham, and I'm asking you to do the same. | Peter, Darline Graham is a principled conservative leader and a strong advocate for South Carolina families. And I am proud to give her my full support. Darline’s brother and my dear friend, Lindsey Graham, served South Carolina with distinction. Darline carries that same sense of duty into this fight in her own way. Peter, she is not a career politician. She spent nearly thirty years serving South Carolina before she ever ran for anything, and she stepped into this race the same way she has approached everything else in her life: because it was needed, not because she wanted the title. Her Democrat opponent, with the help of the National Democrats, has raised nearly $11 million to try to flip this seat. Hollywood donors and DC insiders think that if they can pour enough money into this race, they can elect the most radical Democrat ever nominated for statewide office in South Carolina. Every attack ad between now and November is designed to convince South Carolina that her Democrat opponent isn’t a radical, paid gun control advocate or a leader of “White Women for Kamala Harris.” Darline’s Democrat opponent opposed South Carolina's law keeping girls' sports for girls. If she’s elected, she’ll back expanding the U.S. Supreme Court. We know better, but right now, Darline doesn’t have the same resources to set the record straight. Darline has already proved she can lead in just a few short months in the Senate, and I know she will continue representing South Carolina with the same purpose and commitment her brother did. South Carolina deserves a senator who has already spent a lifetime proving she will fight for it. Thank you, Tom Cotton | | Paid for by Darline Graham Majority Fund, a joint fundraising committee authorized by and composed of Darline for Senate, Fund for America's Future, Security is Strength PAC, and NRSC. 228 S. As fun as it sounds, there’s more to it. When you chip in $5 – about the price of a happy hour beer – it sets us up to keep this seat blue and reach voters. Let me explain.
Long before I ever walked into the world of politics, I was pouring my energy into the Wynkoop, Colorado's first brewpub. Our flagship brews were Timberline Pale Ale and Sagebrush Stout (with just the faintest hint of a prairie bouquet). We sold them for just $2.25 a pint — 50 cents less than a pint of an import.
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/138756327/645085034/927086807?amounts=5,10,15,25,50,100&amount=5&refcode=email_090726_beerloversday&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMTAvMS83MjY1OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJkMDgyMDQ1NC0wYWFiLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTkzM2IiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=yCilQrD5XKfvG-3R2JMEcKMfJ2YiHgj8ynKlOSlZF9Q=)
Wynkoop was more than just a business venture for me. It was about creating a gathering place for people of all backgrounds and opinions. I truly believed there wasn't a single problem that couldn't be sorted out over a pint of fresh beer.
I didn’t run for office for fame, money, or power. I ran partly because I didn’t want to have a boss. But the main reason: I wanted to bring people together to solve problems. And that’s exactly what we’ve done.
I ran for the Senate on that same idea — to get things done.
We’ve invested billions to confront the climate crisis, lowered prescription drug costs, and made investments to rebuild our infrastructure. We’ve brought thousands of good-paying manufacturing jobs back to America, and worked to make housing more affordable. _And we’re not done yet._
**But look, National Republicans are throwing everything they’ve got at us. They’re determined to flip this seat back to red and roll back the progress we’ve worked so hard for. We’re going to need all the help we can get to keep Colorado blue and keep serving folks like you.**
**_[So in honor of National Beer Lover's Day, we’re asking you to contribute $5 — _about the price of two pints at Wynkoop back in the day!_ — to help our team defend this must-hold seat and take back the Senate.](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/138756328/645085035/927086807?amounts=5,10,15,25,50,100&amount=5&refcode=email_090726_beerloversday&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMTAvMS83MjY1OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJkMDgyMDQ1NC0wYWFiLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTkzM2IiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=yCilQrD5XKfvG-3R2JMEcKMfJ2YiHgj8ynKlOSlZF9Q=)_**

When you chip in $5 – about the price of a happy hour beer – it sets us up to keep this seat blue and reach voters. Let me explain. Long before I ever walked into the world of politics, I was pouring my energy into the Wynkoop, Colorado's first brewpub. Our flagship brews were Timberline Pale Ale and Sagebrush Stout (with just the faintest hint of a prairie bouquet). We sold them for just $2.25 a pint — 50 cents less than a pint of an import. = Wynkoop was more than just a business venture for me. It was about creating a gathering place for people of all backgrounds and opinions. I truly believed there wasn't a single problem that couldn't be sorted out over a pint of fresh beer. [1]Justice Democrats

Peter,

It’s Labor Day, and as corporations continue to buy even more power in
Congress and the most corrupt White House in U.S. history, there’s no
better time to come together and support workers.

Corporate super PACs and billionaire megadonors continue to use their
influence in Washington to block workers from gaining the economic power
their labor deserves. It’s 2026, and the federal minimum wage is still
stuck at $7.25 — the last time it was raised was almost 20 years ago.

While wages have stagnated and corporate profits have exponentially
increased along with the costs of living, working-class people are
struggling to afford the basics like housing, healthcare, gas, and
groceries. Everything is more expensive, so why isn't our labor?

At the same time, corporate interests have continued to fuel ongoing
attacks on workers’ ability to organize and form unions, collectively
bargain, build power in their workplaces, and earn a living wage. In many
places, labor laws are being reversed, and regulations are being lifted,
all in the name of profit and at the expense of working people.

[ https://go.justicedemocrats.com/go/141157?refcode=jd-em20260907-38240&t=1002&akid=38240%2E1203867%2EYZocaf ]Every worker deserves a union,
Peter. If you agree, make a contribution to the
Emergency Workplace Organizing Committee (EWOC) this Labor Day to help
workers build their power.

Every dollar to EWOC helps organize and train non-union workers and win
safer workplaces, better conditions, and equality for themselves and their
co-workers.

[ https://go.justicedemocrats.com/go/141157?refcode=jd-em20260907-38240&t=1003&akid=38240%2E1203867%2EYZocaf ]Contribute

Thanks for anything you can pitch in to support workers today as we keep
up our fight to elect more champions for the working class to Congress.

United we bargain, divided we beg. And workers of the world are done
begging.

In solidarity,

Justice Democrats

I was 17-years-old the first time I raised my right hand and took an oath to support and defend the Constitution against all enemies, foreign and domestic.
I took those words, and that responsibility, seriously every day for the next 4 decades. When I was an intelligence officer. When I was deployed to Afghanistan. When I became an Admiral. And as a member of the president’s National Security Council.

| | Peter,
---
I'm going to be blunt with you.

We are closer to losing this country than most people are willing to admit.

Not someday. Not "if things keep going this way."

Right now.

And the scariest part?

It's not happening in Washington. It's happening in classrooms.

High schools. Colleges.

Places where the next generation is being shaped -- or more accurately... reshaped.

If you've ever looked at what's coming out of our schools and thought: _" What happened to this country?" _

You're not wrong. You're seeing it clearly.

Because while most people are arguing online... while they're hoping things will turn around... while they're waiting for the next election to fix everything...

The other side is doing something far more dangerous.

They're raising the next generation.

Earlier. Faster. And with zero resistance in most places.

That's how countries are lost.

Slowly. Then all at once.

But here's the thing that should give a patriot like you hope...

There is one place where that trend is actually being challenged.

_And it shouldn 't even exist. _

**Just one year ago, Turning Point USA 's high school program -- which is now called "Club America" -- was in about 1,200 schools.**
That alone felt like a miracle.

Because starting even ONE chapter today takes courage most adults don't have.

Conservative students get mocked. Targeted. Threatened. Shut down.

And yet...

_They stepped up anyway. _

About that time, Charlie called me.

He didn't sound optimistic... He sounded urgent.

"Andrew, we've got to move faster."

I told him we were. He stopped me.

"No. You're not thinking what I'm thinking. I want to be in 35,000 high schools."

I actually laughed.

"Charlie... there aren't even 35,000 high schools in America."

"Okay," he said. "How many are there?"

"About 27,000."

And without hesitation: "Good. Let's do 27,000."

I remember sitting there thinking to myself... we're barely in 1,200 schools.

We didn't have the staff. We didn't have the infrastructure. We didn't even have the roadmap yet.

But Charlie wasn't fazed.

_" We'll figure it out." _

That was him.

He didn't wait for perfect conditions.

Because he knew something most people don't want to face: If we wait... _we lose everything. _

And now?

Less than a year later...

**We 're in 3,300 schools. **

**Thirteen percent of all high schools in America. **

**Eight states are now backing this effort to put a Club America chapter in every high school statewide. **

_That shouldn 't be possible. _

Not in this environment. Not with the level of hostility these students face every single day.

And yet... it's still happening.

_But Peter, here 's the part you need to understand: _

This is not a victory. It's a foothold.

_Because in the other 87% of schools? _

There is no resistance. None.

Just one-sided propaganda from the Left.

One-sided pressure on kids who are too young to even realize what's happening to them.

That's the reality.

The question isn't whether we're fighting. We are.

The question is whether it's enough.

Because right now, the students stepping up through Club America...

They're not the majority. _They 're the exception. _

They're the ones willing to take the heat.

The ones willing to stand alone.

The ones willing to risk being targeted just to say: _" I love this country." _

Everything they need to actually stand their ground.

Not symbolically. For real.

They've already made the decision to lead.

All they're waiting on... is you and me.

**Each activism kit costs $25. That 's it. **

name: Mark Ronchetti
subject: Is Deb Haaland Ducking the Debate?
body:
Plus, One NM Race Is Coming Down to the Wire | New episode for dpwillis67@gmail.com

| | | | | |
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/6BlK70bhYc8?e=567664f14c&c2id=f551a60afe6194f7ea2dcf92821ad62e)
| | | | | | Is Deb Haaland Ducking the Debate?

KOB says the New Mexico governor’s debate is set for October 8.Deb Haaland’s campaign says: Not so fast.
And with early voting beginning before that proposed debate date, we think there’s a much bigger question here: Shouldn’t New Mexico voters get to see Deb Haaland and Gregg Hull face each other BEFORE they start casting ballots?
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/2xvGRXJlAY9?e=567664f14c&c2id=f551a60afe6194f7ea2dcf92821ad62e)
| |

🔥 THE HAALAND-HULL DEBATE DRAMAKOB announced that Haaland and Hull would meet live in its Albuquerque studio on October 8. Then Haaland campaign manager Dylan MacArthur publicly pushed back, saying the campaign had already told KOB that the week of October 5 would not work and had offered six other dates.
So... do we actually have a debate? We break down why we think this probably WILL get resolved — because KOB, Haaland and Hull all have reasons to make it happen.
But Krysty makes the case that the debate should happen in September, before early voting begins. And Mark brings some unique perspective to this one. He’s been on that debate stage, negotiated these debates and dealt directly with New Mexico television stations during statewide campaigns.
The bottom line: This shouldn’t be about what works best for the campaigns.It should be about what works best for VOTERS.

📊 NEW MEXICO’S CD2 RACE COULD BE A NAIL-BITERWe also dig into new numbers in the race between Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez and Republican Greg Cunningham.The SurveyUSA/KOB numbers discussed on the show:Vasquez: 46%
Cunningham: 43%That’s a three-point race before the biggest wave of campaign spending really gets underway.Krysty thinks this could be the closest major race on New Mexico’s ballot — and potentially close enough that we may not know the winner on election night.
---
| [STREAM NOW](https://us.list-manage.com/WCx4FDlRbUm?e=567664f14c&c2id=f551a60afe6194f7ea2dcf92821ad62e)
---
| |

💰 THE ECONOMY MAY BE THE GOP’S BIGGEST PROBLEMHere’s where we connect several stories that look unrelated — but really aren’t.Energy.
Diesel.
Inflation.
Consumer buying power.
And November.
Diesel prices remain painfully high, and that matters far beyond what you pay at the pump. Trucks move virtually everything we buy, which means higher transportation costs eventually show up throughout the economy.Meanwhile, the New Mexico economic polling we discuss is bleak:Only about 17% rate the state economy good or excellent.43% call it fair.38% say it’s poor.
That creates a serious political problem for Republicans.
Voters expected the economy and their purchasing power to improve. There ARE positive economic indicators, but if families still feel squeezed every time they buy groceries, fill the tank or pay their bills, politicians can’t simply tell them everything is great. And nationally, the political environment is showing warning signs for Republicans.
Spoiler alert: Mark thinks this is going to be an uphill midterm election for the GOP.
🇺🇸 TRUMP HAS A MASSIVE WAR CHESTPresident Trump says he has close to $1 BILLION in his super PAC and could deploy $400-$500 million in the midterms.That money could matter enormously in close Senate and House races.But we get into the question that drives Mark crazy:How much money will Republicans have to spend rescuing candidates in races that shouldn’t have been this difficult in the first place?
Texas is exhibit A.
A statewide race in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat statewide in decades is suddenly competitive — and Trump’s political operation may have to pour tens of millions into protecting it. Good candidates matter. Bad candidates can turn safe races into expensive disasters.
---
| [STREAM NOW](https://us.list-manage.com/GGNR9CGUFCM?e=567664f14c&c2id=f551a60afe6194f7ea2dcf92821ad62e)
---
| |

🍽️ FOOD STAMP REFORM SHOWING RESULTS
Here’s one piece of fiscal news worth watching. The Wall Street Journal analysis we discuss reports food stamp enrollment fell from roughly 42 million Americans in May 2025 to 36 million in May 2026. Projected spending has also fallen significantly below previous forecasts.Our position is pretty simple: Help people who genuinely need help.But taxpayers also deserve a government that verifies eligibility, reduces errors and treats their money like it actually matters.
🚨 IS JOHN FETTERMAN’S OWN PARTY TURNING ON HIM?This one fascinated us. A Wall Street Journal story paints a brutal picture of Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman, relying in part on former staffers and other unnamed sources to describe dysfunction behind the scenes.Mark immediately saw a political hit piece.
Why?
Fetterman has increasingly broken with the loudest voices in his own party, particularly on Israel and several cultural issues. Now he’s more popular with some Republicans than members of his own party. We break down the fascinating question of what happens next. Could Fetterman eventually become an independent? Could he switch parties? Or does he simply walk away from Washington?
🍣 AND FINALLY... WE APOLOGIZE TO SUSHI LOVERSKrysty did NOT want this story in the show. Mark insisted.Scientists examined a recent sample of tuna and found an absolutely horrifying prevalence of parasitic worms. Krysty loves raw tuna.Krysty would now like to return to the time before she knew this information.We’ll leave it there. 😂
🐻 SUNDAY GAME DAY: THE BEARS FIGHT BACKWe finish with our bears at nearly 11,000 feet in Angel Fire.One is apparently VERY ready for hibernation. Another apparently decided he had had enough of being filmed — and launched a surprise attack directly on our camera. We have the video. It’s fantastic.

KOB says the New Mexico governor’s debate is set for October 8.Deb Haaland’s campaign says: Not so fast. And with early voting beginning before that proposed debate date, we think there’s a much bigger question here: Shouldn’t New Mexico voters get to see Deb Haaland and Gregg Hull face each other BEFORE they start casting ballots? | | 🔥 THE HAALAND-HULL DEBATE DRAMAKOB announced that Haaland and Hull would meet live in its Albuquerque studio on October 8. Then Haaland campaign manager Dylan MacArthur publicly pushed back, saying the campaign had already told KOB that the week of October 5 would not work and had offered six other dates. So... do we actually have a debate? We break down why we think this probably WILL get resolved — because KOB, Haaland and Hull all have reasons to make it happen. But Krysty makes the case that the debate should happen in September, before early voting begins. And Mark brings some unique perspective to this one. He’s been on that debate stage, negotiated these debates and dealt directly with New Mexico television stations during statewide campaigns. The bottom line: This shouldn’t be about what works best for the campaigns.It should be about what works best for VOTERS. 📊 NEW MEXICO’S CD2 RACE COULD BE A NAIL-BITERWe also dig into new numbers in the race between Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez and Republican Greg Cunningham.The SurveyUSA/KOB numbers discussed on the show:Vasquez: 46% Cunningham: 43%That’s a three-point race before the biggest wave of campaign spending really gets underway.Krysty thinks this could be the closest major race on New Mexico’s ballot — and potentially close enough that we may not know the winner on election night. | | | 💰 THE ECONOMY MAY BE THE GOP’S BIGGEST PROBLEMHere’s where we connect several stories that look unrelated — but really aren’t.Energy. Diesel. Inflation. Consumer buying power. And November. Diesel prices remain painfully high, and that matters far beyond what you pay at the pump. Trucks move virtually everything we buy, which means higher transportation costs eventually show up throughout the economy.Meanwhile, the New Mexico economic polling we discuss is bleak:Only about 17% rate the state economy good or excellent.43% call it fair.38% say it’s poor. That creates a serious political problem for Republicans. Voters expected the economy and their purchasing power to improve. There ARE positive economic indicators, but if families still feel squeezed every time they buy groceries, fill the tank or pay their bills, politicians can’t simply tell them everything is great. And nationally, the political environment is showing warning signs for Republicans. Spoiler alert: Mark thinks this is going to be an uphill midterm election for the GOP. 🇺🇸 TRUMP HAS A MASSIVE WAR CHESTPresident Trump says he has close to $1 BILLION in his super PAC and could deploy $400-$500 million in the midterms.That money could matter enormously in close Senate and House races.But we get into the question that drives Mark crazy:How much money will Republicans have to spend rescuing candidates in races that shouldn’t have been this difficult in the first place? Texas is exhibit A. A statewide race in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat statewide in decades is suddenly competitive — and Trump’s political operation may have to pour tens of millions into protecting it. Good candidates matter. Bad candidates can turn safe races into expensive disasters. | | | 🍽️ FOOD STAMP REFORM SHOWING RESULTS Here’s one piece of fiscal news worth watching. The Wall Street Journal analysis we discuss reports food stamp enrollment fell from roughly 42 million Americans in May 2025 to 36 million in May 2026. Projected spending has also fallen significantly below previous forecasts.Our position is pretty simple: Help people who genuinely need help.But taxpayers also deserve a government that verifies eligibility, reduces errors and treats their money like it actually matters. 🚨 IS JOHN FETTERMAN’S OWN PARTY TURNING ON HIM?This one fascinated us. A Wall Street Journal story paints a brutal picture of Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman, relying in part on former staffers and other unnamed sources to describe dysfunction behind the scenes.Mark immediately saw a political hit piece. Why? Fetterman has increasingly broken with the loudest voices in his own party, particularly on Israel and several cultural issues. Now he’s more popular with some Republicans than members of his own party. We break down the fascinating question of what happens next. Could Fetterman eventually become an independent? Could he switch parties? Or does he simply walk away from Washington? 🍣 AND FINALLY... WE APOLOGIZE TO SUSHI LOVERSKrysty did NOT want this story in the show. Mark insisted.Scientists examined a recent sample of tuna and found an absolutely horrifying prevalence of parasitic worms. Krysty loves raw tuna.Krysty would now like to return to the time before she knew this information.We’ll leave it there. 😂 🐻 SUNDAY GAME DAY: THE BEARS FIGHT BACKWe finish with our bears at nearly 11,000 feet in Angel Fire.One is apparently VERY ready for hibernation. Another apparently decided he had had enough of being filmed — and launched a surprise attack directly on our camera. We have the video. It’s fantastic. | | | ✅ LIKE on ✅ hit the bell ✅ FORWARD to anyone who thinks the grocery stores will just fail on their own ✅ at NoDoubtAboutItPodcast.com | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | © 2026 Choose Adventure Media. name: Rep. Vikki Goodwin
subject: Happy Labor Day
disclaimer_text: paid for by the Vikki Goodwin Campaign, Allen Biehl, Treasurer
body:
The most valuable part of our economy isn't data centers. It's you.| | |
---
| | | [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/138757441/645088788/24352196?refcode=du_em_090726_lg&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNTAvMS8xMDM3NDAiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiYmMyY2NmNTQtMTRhYi1mMTExLTliMzMtMDAyMjQ4MmE5MzNiIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=-Mxn5fOxQpru3_33csc_bWpRyS8dXLooDztKMNJFaFA=)
---
Peter, Today is Labor Day — a day to recognize, honor, and celebrate the working people who built this country and keep it running every single day. That includes the nurses working a double shift right now. The grocery store clerks restocking shelves this morning. The sanitation workers, the bus drivers, the cooks, and the caregivers who don't get the day off because the bills don't take holidays. Here's what I believe:**the most valuable part of our economy isn't our infrastructure or our GDP. It's people. It's you.**
---
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/138757442/645088789/24352196?refcode=du_em_090726_i1&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNTAvMS8xMDM3NDAiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiYmMyY2NmNTQtMTRhYi1mMTExLTliMzMtMDAyMjQ4MmE5MzNiIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=-Mxn5fOxQpru3_33csc_bWpRyS8dXLooDztKMNJFaFA=)
---
That's why the labor groups who fight for Texas workers — for fair wages, safe conditions, and a seat at the table — have put their trust in this campaign. It's why I am running on a platform built around one question: **Does this help working Texas families?**
**Clean drinking water —** not diverted to cool servers for tech billionaires while Texas families are left with dried-up wells and rising water bills. Our water belongs to the people of Texas, not to the highest corporate bidder.
**Affordable healthcare for every Texan** , not just the ones who can afford it. Dan Patrick has controlled the Texas Senate for more than a decade. He had every opportunity to act. He chose not to. As Lieutenant Governor, I will use this office to change that.
**An end to the corruption that has cost families everything** — Dan Patrick has spent years protecting insiders, pocketing money from the same groups he was supposed to hold accountable, and letting property taxes crush the families who are just trying to stay in their homes. That ends when we win.
None of this is a campaign promise. It's a record of where I've stood, and a commitment to where I will stand when we win in November.
**Today, I hope you get to rest. I hope you get to spend time with the people you love. And if you're working, thank you.**
Happy Labor Day.
In solidarity,
Rep. Vikki Goodwin

That includes the nurses working a double shift right now. The grocery store clerks restocking shelves this morning. The sanitation workers, the bus drivers, the cooks, and the caregivers who don't get the day off because the bills don't take holidays. Here's what I believe:the most valuable part of our economy isn't our infrastructure or our GDP. It's people. It's you. = That's why the labor groups who fight for Texas workers — for fair wages, safe conditions, and a seat at the table — have put their trust in this campaign. It's why I am running on a platform built around one question: Does this help working Texas families? Clean drinking water — not diverted to cool servers for tech billionaires while Texas families are left with dried-up wells and rising water bills. Dan Patrick has controlled the Texas Senate for more than a decade. He had every opportunity to act. He chose not to. As Lieutenant Governor, I will use this office to change that. There is an old political saying: **" It's the economy."** As America approaches the 2026 midterm elections, that message may be more important than ever. Americans care about the border. They care about crime. They care about national security, religious liberty, education, the Constitution, and the direction of our culture. Those issues matter greatly. But there is another issue confronting Americans every single day: **Can I afford to live?** Can I afford groceries? Can I fill up my truck? Can my family afford a house? Can I pay my insurance? Can I keep my small business open? Can I afford electricity? Can I raise my children without living paycheck to paycheck?
